Comment: Lift ladder from magic carpet to 3S: 26 types in six families, tiers 1-5 gate by economy.json acts. Capacity is the delivered pph the lift system uses directly; for circulating lifts CarrierSpacingM = seats * 3600 * LineSpeedMs / CapacityPph so the carrier count and capex follow from the line length (reversible and rail systems carry 0: two cars or trains regardless of length). Capex is split into per-km line, per-tower, drive/return terminals, per-carrier and cabin barn; construction.json adds the site work on top. Figures are 2020s European/North American installed costs in USD; names are original.

lifts.Comment: Beginner conveyor belt: 0.8 m/s, ~1,200 riders/h, 30-150 m long on grades under 8 deg. Sits on the ground on a light frame every 25 m, so it has no real span. Installed cost is about 1,500 USD per metre plus the drive station.
Conveyor under a polycarbonate gallery: 1.0 m/s, ~1,500 riders/h, up to 250 m. The gallery keeps the belt clear of drift and sheltered from wind; cost roughly doubles per metre.
Handle tow: a 2 m/s rope with handles every 12 m, ~600 riders/h, up to 300 m. The cheapest lift there is (a few hundred thousand per km) but hard on beginners' arms.
Disc (button) lift with retractable spring boxes: 2.2 m/s, ~900 riders/h, discs every 8.8 m, lines to 900 m on grades to 24 deg. The single-rider surface lift of small European village hills.
Two-rider T-bar: 2.5 m/s, 1,200 riders/h with a T every 15 m, up to 1,200 m and 350 m vertical on grades to 25 deg. The Act I village lift; about 1.3 M USD installed per km including terminals.

High-speed glacier-style T-bar: 3.0 m/s, 1,400 riders/h, up to 1,800 m and 450 m vertical. Needs a top attendant on the long line. The workhorse of glacier and wind-exposed plateaus where chairs would be on hold.
Single chair: 2.0 m/s, 600 riders/h with a chair every 12 m. A 1940s-1960s design still found on heritage lines; the cheapest chair to build (about 2 M USD per km installed).
Double chair: 2.3 m/s, 1,200 riders/h with a chair every 13.8 m, lines to 1,800 m. About 2.5 M USD per km installed; the classic small-resort chair.
Triple chair: 2.3 m/s, 1,800 riders/h, chairs every 13.8 m. A bottom loader joins the operator once three riders board at a time.

Fixed-grip quad: 2.3 m/s, 2,400 riders/h with a chair every 13.8 m, up to 2,200 m and 600 m vertical, 300 kW drive. About 3.7 M USD for a 1 km line installed. The Silberhorn reference lift and the baseline of the Act IV trap.

Detachable quad: 5.0 m/s on the line, 1.0 m/s through the terminals, 2,800 riders/h with a chair every 25.7 m, lines to 3,000 m. Terminals with detach/attach rails cost four times a fixed-grip pair, the line 2.2x per km, and opex per hour is about double: the Act IV trap in numbers.
Six-seat detachable: 5.0 m/s, 3,600 riders/h with a chair every 30 m, 700 kW drive. The standard front-side lift of a mid-size 2020s resort at roughly 10 M USD per km installed.
Eight-seat detachable: 5.5 m/s, 4,800 riders/h with a chair every 33 m, 900 kW drive, loading carpet practically mandatory. The highest-capacity chair built today; 12-14 M USD per km.

Fixed-grip quad with factory bubbles: same 2.3 m/s / 2,400 riders/h as the plain quad, but riders sit out of the wind and snow (exposure 0.45 instead of 0.85). Bubbles add drag in a crosswind, so the hold comes 5 km/h earlier.

Pulse gondola: fixed-grip 8-passenger cabins in groups of four; the rope runs at 4 m/s and slows to walking pace while a group is in the stations, so the average spacing works out to 144 m and 800 riders/h. Cheap cabin capacity for a village-to-mid-station link.

Monocable detachable gondola with 8-passenger cabins: 5.0 m/s, 2,800 riders/h with a cabin every 51 m, up to 3,500 m and 1,000 m vertical. Cabins stop for 12 s in the load zone and sleep in a barn; 14 M USD per km installed.
Monocable gondola with 10-passenger cabins: 6.0 m/s, 3,600 riders/h with a cabin every 60 m, 1 MW drive, lines to 4,000 m. The mid-2020s standard for a base-to-summit access lift.

Bicable (one track rope, one haul rope) gondola with 15-passenger cabins: 6.0 m/s, 3,000 riders/h with a cabin every 108 m, spans to 700 m on five towers per km, holds at 85 km/h. About 18 M USD per km installed.

Funitel: two haul-rope loops 3.2 m apart carrying 24-passenger cabins on a wide double grip, 7.0 m/s, 3,600 riders/h with a cabin every 168 m. The wide grip is why it keeps running at 100 km/h when every monocable is on hold.

Combined lift: alternating 6-seat chairs and 8-passenger cabins on one monocable rope (average 7 per carrier), 5.0 m/s, 3,400 riders/h with a carrier every 37 m. Skiers keep their skis on the chairs, pedestrians and children ride the cabins; the two carrier types make it the most complex terminal in the detachable class.

Reversible aerial tramway: two 80-passenger cabins shuttling on fixed track ropes at 10 m/s, 90 s dwell, about 900 riders/h on a 1 km line (capacity falls with length). One or two towers per line, spans to 3 km, so it is the first lift that can cross the Silberhorn gorge; tower sections fly in by heavy-lift helicopter.

Large reversible tramway: two 150-passenger cabins at 12 m/s with a 2 min dwell, about 1,500 riders/h on a 1 km line, 2.4 MW drive, 1,800 m vertical in one section. The summit-lift format of the big Alpine glacier resorts; 30-40 M USD for a 1.5 km line.

Tricable detachable gondola (two track ropes, one haul rope): 32-passenger cabins at 7.5 m/s every 192 m, 4,500 riders/h, spans to 3 km on one or two towers per km, runs to 110 km/h wind. 50-80 M USD for a 1-2 km line; the only circulating lift that crosses the gorge. The Act V trap: it opens the east bowl, which has no lodge and no parking.

Two 120-passenger rail cars counterbalanced on one haul rope, 10 m/s (36 km/h) on a passing loop, 90 s dwell, about 1,800 riders/h. Grades to 50 deg on a track bed with a support every 33 m: no span and no wind hold, but 10 M USD per km of track plus stations, and it needs a driver.

Electric rack railway: 100-passenger two-car trains climbing at 5.5 m/s (20 km/h) on a rack rail, grades to 25 deg (about 45 percent), lines to 6 km. Two trains on a 2 km line give about 800 riders/h. The classic mountain access of the Swiss and Austrian pre-war resorts; strong summer ridership.

Short reversible inclined lift: one 25-passenger car on a 300 m track at 3 m/s with a 40 s dwell, about 500 riders/h, automatic operation with a single attendant. Links a parking level or village street to the base area; grades to 42 deg.

options.Comment: Polycarbonate bubbles on every chair: riders sit out of wind and snow (+0.15 comfort), the chair costs about 18 percent more, and the extra sail area brings the wind hold 5 km/h earlier.
Induction-charged seat heating on detachable chairs (the chair picks up power in the terminal). Listed on the detachable types only; adds about 4 percent to operating power.
Moving carpet in the load zone that brings riders up to chair speed: fewer misloads and stops, about 8 percent more delivered capacity, and beginners board with confidence.
Floodlights on the line and terminals for night skiing on the runs the lift serves.
Rope-catcher and sheave-battery fairings plus carrier deflectors that keep the rope in the sheaves in a crosswind: the hold threshold rises by 10 km/h.
Heated cabin storage: cabins go out dry and warm in the morning instead of iced; the extra heating load shows up as opex.
Line-side access points and cabin repeaters for enclosed carriers; a small comfort bonus and a small recurring data cost.
Bars that close and lock on leaving the terminal and open before the unload ramp: fewer stops for children and beginners, required by code in some jurisdictions.
